questions.title: What qualifies as an "enforcement proceeding" under FOIA Exemption 7(A), and do long-running counterterrorism investigations count?
questions.question_body: The panel says ongoing criminal investigations count as "proceedings" and that the government can meet its burden by attesting to their existence (citing CREW and Juarez). Here, the FBI relied on both public and ex parte declarations to say the investigation into Farahi is ongoing. I'm confused about the line between a general counterterrorism investigation that could go on for years and a "concrete prospective law enforcement proceeding" that CREW seems to require. What makes an investigation sufficiently concrete to qualify as a pending or reasonably anticipated proceeding for 7(A) purposes, especially when no indictment has issued after many years?

questions.title: How much deference does the court give the FBI’s assertions in national security FOIA cases, and what evidentiary showing is still required?
questions.question_body: The opinion emphasizes deference to the FBI, especially where national security is implicated (CNSS; Campbell). But it also says the agency must show a rational nexus to law-enforcement duties and a link to a possible security risk or violation (Pratt/Campbell), and must attest to the existence of ongoing proceedings (CREW). In practice, what is the threshold detail required in public filings before the court will accept ex parte material to fill in the gaps? Is a largely conclusory public assertion that "investigations remain ongoing" acceptable if supplemented ex parte, or does CREW require more public specificity?

questions.title: Did the court miscite FOIA by referring to § 552(b)(7)(B) instead of (b)(7)(A), and if so, does that matter?
questions.question_body: In Section IV.B, the panel quotes the interference standard and cites 5 U.S.C. § 552(b)(7)(B), but Exemption 7(B) is about depriving a person of a fair trial, while 7(A) is the interference-with-proceedings exemption at issue here. Is this just a typographical error without substantive effect, or could it create ambiguity about the standard the court applied?

questions.title: When can a district court require "refresh" declarations to address staleness, and what makes an initial 7(A) showing become stale?
questions.question_body: The district court initially denied summary judgment without prejudice and required updated declarations due to the passage of time, then granted summary judgment after receiving the Bender updates. Is there a doctrinal standard for when a 7(A) declaration becomes too stale to support summary judgment? How much time or what kinds of changed circumstances trigger a duty to supplement, and is this within the district court’s discretion?

questions.title: What are the rules for category-by-category withholdings and Vaughn submissions under 7(A), and how did Farahi forfeit that challenge?
questions.question_body: The opinion briefly mentions that when an agency withholds on a category basis, the categories must be sufficiently distinct to assess the exemption (CREW; Gallant). The court says Farahi forfeited any overbreadth argument by not specifically explaining why the FBI’s categories were improper. What level of specificity must a requester provide to preserve a challenge to categorical withholdings or the adequacy of a Vaughn index in a 7(A) case, and what kinds of categorical descriptions have courts found too vague?

questions.title: How does the segregability requirement work when non-exempt bits are interspersed throughout highly sensitive records?
questions.question_body: The court upholds withholding in full because any non-exempt material is interspersed line-by-line and not "reasonably segregable" (Mead; Perioperative Services). What is the governing test for when line-by-line redactions are deemed unreasonable, and how do courts evaluate an agency's ex parte explanation that further segregation would be meaningless? Are agencies required to release context-free names/dates or boilerplate headings if those could be extracted without harm, or is the "meaningless snippet" concept dispositive?

questions.title: To what extent may courts rely on ex parte, in camera declarations in FOIA cases, and does the requester’s failure to object waive later challenges?
questions.question_body: The district court accepted ex parte declarations; Farahi didn’t object, and on appeal the panel says he can’t challenge reliance on them. What is the doctrinal basis for using ex parte submissions to decide FOIA cases (especially segregability and 7(A) issues), and how does a requester preserve objections without forcing disclosure of the very material at issue? Are there best practices or limits (e.g., requiring maximum feasible public summaries) that courts enforce before turning to ex parte review?

questions.title: Can adverse information used in immigration proceedings affect the 7(A) analysis in a separate FOIA case?
questions.question_body: The panel references allegations and evidence from Farahi’s immigration proceedings (e.g., ties to designated terrorist organizations and specific individuals) as contextual support for the FBI’s ongoing-investigation claim. Is it proper for a FOIA court to rely on allegations from related civil or immigration matters to buttress the existence and breadth of a law-enforcement investigation under 7(A), or should the analysis be confined to the agency’s FOIA declarations and Vaughn materials?
